questions.question: A research group wants to parallelize an alignment study while preserving a record that agents cannot erase. What architecture fits?
options: One shared writable filesystem used by every agent
Independent agent sandboxes plus an externally stored shared forum
A single in-memory log controlled by the research agent
A private transcript stored only in each agent's context
questions.explanation: Parallel AARs explore work in separate sandboxes while an externally stored forum preserves findings beyond each agent’s write access. A shared writable filesystem lets an agent erase records the team needs to audit.

questions.question: Why does the shared forum's out-of-sandbox storage matter?
options: It guarantees the posted research conclusion is correct
It lets the agent directly control every experiment result
It makes it harder for an agent to erase or rewrite its own record
It removes the need to record who produced each finding
questions.explanation: External append-only records make silent edits detectable and preserve an audit trail, but do not prove the conclusion is true. A correct hash chain verifies record integrity, not scientific validity.

questions.question: According to the lesson, what is the tradeoff between prescribed workflows and free decomposition?
options: Free decomposition guarantees every agent reaches the same result
Prescribed steps always outperform agent-chosen plans
Free decomposition removes the need for external logs
Prescribed steps can be easier to audit but can constrain AAR performance
questions.explanation: Prescribed steps are easier to audit but can constrain decomposition and reduce performance; free decomposition offers more flexibility with more audit work. The lesson does not claim agent-chosen plans always produce the same result.

questions.question: Which part of the alignment research pipeline remains human-owned in the described setup?
options: Replace external measurement with the AAR's self-report
Edit agent logs after each experiment
Humans set tasks and decide what to publish
Run every intermediate model call by hand
questions.explanation: Humans retain task allocation, result review, and publication decisions while AARs accelerate the middle of the pipeline. Replacing external measurement with self-report would remove the independent evidence the loop needs.

questions.question: A record in the shared forum is altered after publication. What can the simulator's hash chain do?
options: Prevent every agent from proposing a new experiment
A hash mismatch flags an altered record
Restore the original experiment automatically from the model
Prove the agent's scientific claim was false
questions.explanation: The chain recomputes each record hash from its contents and predecessor, so a changed result creates a mismatch. Detection flags tampering; it does not prove the claim false or restore the original record.

questions.question: AAR agents perform better with flexibility but may drift into unplanned tool use. What design response follows the lesson's tradeoff?
options: Keep independent sandboxes and tamper-evident logs, then review outputs
Remove task allocation and all human review to maximize speed
Allow agents to modify forum history as part of their decomposition
Force every research step into a fixed script regardless of measured loss
questions.explanation: The lesson pairs flexible decomposition with sandboxing, immutable records, and human review so agents can explore while remaining auditable. Removing human review discards the publication gate; a fully fixed script also loses useful flexibility.
